320.heading: Greek Language History
320.text:
Greek Language History

Greek is one of the oldest members of the Indo-European family of languages. Other members of this family are Sanskrit, which is older, and Latin and its descendants (the Romance languages: French, Spanish, etc.), which are younger. English is derived from the Teutonic branch and Russian from the Slavic branch of the Indo-European family. Hebrew is found in a totally different family—Semitic languages (Aramaic, Akkadian, Ugaritic etc.).

The Greek language has developed through five stages:

Formative Period — This period extended from "Linear B" (ca 1200 BC) down through the time of Homer (ca 900 BC).
Classical Period — The Classical Period was from the time of Homer down to Alexander the Great (330 BC). There were three dialects during this period (Doric, Aeolic, and Ionic). Attic, a branch of Ionic, became the predominant form in which most of the famous classical Greek authors wrote, such as Plato and Aristotle.
The Koine Period — As Alexander spread the Greek language and culture through the ancient world many of the subtleties of classical Greek were lost. Greek was simplified and changed as it interfaced with other cultures. This common language Greek came to be known as Koine (common) Greek. It was the language used from 300 BC to 300 AD. It was in this language that the Septuagint (the Greek translation of Old Testament), the New Testament and the writings of the early Church fathers were written. The nature of Koine eluded scholars because of its simplicity when compared to Classical Greek, which led some scholars to explain it as a "Holy Ghost" language created just for the Bible. After the Egyptian papyri, inscriptions, and ostraca were found, scholars realized that the New Testament was written in the common everyday language of the people of those times. At points the New Testament will manifest Hebraisms where the influence of Hebrew and/or Aramaic may be seen.
The Byzantine Period — During the Byzantine Period (A.D. 330-1453), Greek was spoken in the eastern half of the Roman empire which was centered in Constantinople.
The Modern Period — The Modern Period dates from 1453 to the present. Modern Greek is closer to Koine than it is to Classical Greek.
(Dana & Mantey, pp. 1ff.; Mounce, pp. 1f.)

320.label: rail stop
320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

In order to correctly pronounce Greek words we need to be able to identify the syllables of the words.

Greek divides words into syllables in almost the same way as English. So if you don't recognize a new word, just try to pronounce it as you would in English. Generally, start at the left and divide after the vowel.

(Mounce, pp. 15ff; Summers, pp. 8, Hewett, p. 4)

topics.label: topic 2
topics.heading: Three Syllable Rules
topics.text:
Three Syllable Rules
1)
There is one vowel or diphthong per syllable. A lone consonant often goes with the following vowel.
2)
Two consonants in a row are divided (except when the second consonant is ν or a consonant pair that is used to begin words).
3)
Two vowels (two diphthongs or a vowel and a diphthong) in a row are split unless the two vowels form a diphthong.

320.label: rail stop
320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

Accents originally indicated the pitch of one's voice but today we use them to denote stress. While accents were not part of the original text, they are helpful for consistent pronunciation and may, at points, differentiate between two similar words.

We will simply learn to recognize them and use them to standardize pronunciation.

(Mounce, pp. 14f.; Summers, p. 9; Machen, pp. 14f.)

topics.label: topic 4
topics.heading: 6 Accent Rules
topics.text:
6 Accent Rules
1)
Nouns are retentive. They attempt to keep their accents on the same syllable.
2)
Verbs are recessive. Their accent recedes towards the first syllable as far as is possible.
3)
If the ultima is long, then the antepenult cannot be accented.
4)
If the ultima is long and the penult is accented, then the accent must be an acute.
5)
If the ultima is short and the penult is both long and accented, the accent must be a circumflex.
6)
If an acute is on the ultima, it becomes a grave when followed by another word.
(Machen, pp. 14f.; Mounce, p. 20)

topics.text:
Words with No Accents

There are several short Greek words which do not have an accent. These words are pronounced as if they were part of the word which accompanies them.

1)
Proclitic: comes before the word which carries the accent.
2)
Enclitic: comes after the word which carries the accent.

768.heading: Introduction
768.text:
Introduction

Accents originally indicated the pitch of one's voice but today we use them to denote stress. While accents were not part of the original text, they are helpful for consistent pronunciation and may, at points, differentiate between two similar words.

We will simply learn to recognize them and use them to standardize pronunciation.

(Mounce, pp. 14f.; Summers, p. 9; Machen, pp. 14f.)

states.text:
6 Accent Rules
1)
Nouns are retentive. They attempt to keep their accents on the same syllable.
2)
Verbs are recessive. Their accent recedes towards the first syllable as far as is possible.
3)
If the ultima is long, then the antepenult cannot be accented.
4)
If the ultima is long and the penult is accented, then the accent must be an acute.
5)
If the ultima is short and the penult is both long and accented, the accent must be a circumflex.
6)
If an acute is on the ultima, it becomes a grave when followed by another word.
(Machen, pp. 14f.; Mounce, p. 20)
Rule 1: Nouns are retentive
Rule 2: Verbs are recessive
Rule 3: Long Ultima, no antepenult accent
ἄνθρωπος
man (antepenult accented, acute)
ἀνθρώπου
man (penult acute—cannot accent antepenult)
ἀνθρώπῳ
man (penult acute—cannot accent antepenult)
Rule 4: Long Ultima, acute penult
Rule 5: Short Ultima, long penult = circumflex
Rule 6: Acute Ultima changed to grave

states.heading: Words with No Accents
states.text:
Words with No Accents

There are several short Greek words which do not have an accent. These words are pronounced as if they were part of the word which accompanies them.

1)
Proclitic: comes before the word which carries the accent.
2)
Enclitic: comes after the word which carries the accent.
Proclitic (before the accented word)
Enclitic (after the accented word)

320.heading: Breathing Marks
320.text:
Breathing Marks

There are two breathing marks which are placed on vowels and diphthongs when they begin words.

1)
Smooth breathing ( ᾿ ): It does not affect pronunciation.
2)
Rough breathing ( ῾ ): Adds an "h" before the sound of the initial vowel.
(Mounce, p. 10; Machen, p. 11; Summers, pp. 8f.)

topics.heading: Punctuation Marks
topics.text:
Punctuation Marks

There are four punctuation marks in Greek. The comma and period are the same as in English.

1) Period ( . )
λόγος.
2) Comma ( , )
λόγος,
3) Colon ( · )
λόγος·
4) Question Mark ( ; )
λόγος;
(Mounce, pp. 13f.; Summers, p. 8; Machen, p. 12)

topics.label: topic 3
topics.heading: Apostrophe
topics.text:
Apostrophe

In English, letters that drop out (elide) are marked with an apostrophe (e.g. it's).

Greek also uses an apostrophe to mark the missing letter(s). The final letter of a preposition, if it is a vowel, is dropped when it precedes a word that begins with a vowel.

διά
+
αὐτοῦ
becomes
δι' αὐτοῦ
(Note the "a" lost is replaced by an apostrophe; Jn 1:3,7 cf. Jn 1:39)

Coronis

Sometimes a final vowel word followed by an initial vowel word will contract together. This is called "Crasis." A coronis ( ᾿ ) is used to retain the breathing of the second word.

καί
+
ἐγώ
becomes
κἀγώ
(Jn 1:31, 33)
(Summers, p. 8)

topics.label: topic 5
topics.heading: Diaeresis
topics.text:
Diaeresis

A diaeresis is placed over the second of two vowels in a row to show that the vowels are to be pronounced separately and not combined as a diphthong. This often occurs in personal or place names. Note the acute accent placement in Isaiah.

Ἠσαΐας
Isaiah (Jn 1:23)
Μωϋσῆς
Moses (Jn 1:45)
Ἀχαΐα
Achaia (Acts 18:12)

Diaeresis

A diaeresis is placed over the second of two vowels in a row to show that the vowels are to be pronounced separately and not combined as a diphthong. This often occurs in personal or place names. Note the acute accent placement in Isaiah.

Breathing Marks

There are two breathing marks which are placed on vowels and diphthongs when they begin words.

1)
Smooth breathing ( ᾿ ): It does not affect pronunciation.
2)
Rough breathing ( ῾ ): Adds an "h" before the sound of the initial vowel.
(Mounce, p. 10; Machen, p. 11; Summers, pp. 8f.)

states.heading: Punctuation Marks
states.text:
Punctuation Marks

There are four punctuation marks in Greek. The comma and period are the same as in English.

1) Period ( . )
λόγος.
2) Comma ( , )
λόγος,
3) Colon ( · )
λόγος·
4) Question Mark ( ; )
λόγος;
(Mounce, pp. 13f.; Summers, p. 8; Machen, p. 12)

states.text:
Apostrophe

In English, letters that drop out (elide) are marked with an apostrophe (e.g. it's).

Greek also uses an apostrophe to mark the missing letter(s). The final letter of a preposition, if it is a vowel, is dropped when it precedes a word that begins with a vowel.

διά
+
αὐτοῦ
becomes
δι' αὐτοῦ
(Note the "a" lost is replaced by an apostrophe; Jn 1:3,7 cf. Jn 1:39)

Noun: names a person, place, thing or idea (e.g. book).

Adjective: a word used to qualify the meaning of the noun (e.g. good book).

Identifying Verbs
Tense:
generally describes the time of action (Present, Future, Past). However, some Greek tenses are used to denote aspect, or type of action, rather than time.
Aspect:
denotes the type of action: Continuous action (the event as a process), Undefined (the event happened) or Perfect (the event happened with effects continuing into the present).
Voice:
Active: subject does the action, Middle: subject does action on or for itself, Passive: subject receives the action.
Mood:
how something is said. Indicative: statement of fact; Subjunctive: desire, probable; Imperative: command; Optative: wish, remote possibility.
Person:
I, we = first person; you = second person; he, she, it, they = third person
Number:
Singular: I, you, he, she, it; Plural: we, they, you (all)

topics.label: topic 4
topics.heading: Nouns
topics.text:
Nouns

Nouns in Greek have gender, number and case.

Gender:

The Greek masculine, feminine, and neuter genders are often indicated by the endings attached to the noun. Abstract nouns and objects that are neither male nor female in English are often marked as either masculine or feminine in Greek.

Number:

as an "s" often marks an English word as being plural, likewise, Greek endings mark whether a noun is singular or plural (e.g. book, books).

Case:

In English we have three cases which are seen in how we use our pronouns.

1)
Subjective or Nominative Case: He=subject (e.g. He did it.)
2)
Objective or Accusative Case: Him = object (e.g. The car hit him.)
3)
Possessive or Genitive Case: His=possessive (e.g. It was his car.)

Greek adds two more:

4)
Dative: the case marking the indirect object (e.g. I told the story to the apostles.)
5)
Vocative: the case of direct address. (e.g. O Lord, save me.)

Endings will be added to the Greek nouns to indicate gender, number and case.

states.heading: Nouns
states.text:
Nouns

Nouns in Greek have gender, number and case.

Gender:

The Greek masculine, feminine, and neuter genders are often indicated by the endings attached to the noun. Abstract nouns and objects that are neither male nor female in English are often marked as either masculine or feminine in Greek.

Number:

as an "s" often marks an English word as being plural, likewise, Greek endings mark whether a noun is singular or plural (e.g. book, books).

Case:

In English we have three cases which are seen in how we use our pronouns.

1)
Subjective or Nominative Case: He=subject (e.g. He did it.)
2)
Objective or Accusative Case: Him = object (e.g. The car hit him.)
3)
Possessive or Genitive Case: His=possessive (e.g. It was his car.)

Greek adds two more:

4)
Dative: the case marking the indirect object (e.g. I told the story to the apostles.)
5)
Vocative: the case of direct address. (e.g. O Lord, save me.)

Endings will be added to the Greek nouns to indicate gender, number and case.

states.label: topic 4
states.heading: Nouns
states.text:
Nouns

Nouns in Greek have gender, number and case.

Gender:

The Greek masculine, feminine, and neuter genders are often indicated by the endings attached to the noun. Abstract nouns and objects that are neither male nor female in English are often marked as either masculine or feminine in Greek.

Number:

as an "s" often marks an English word as being plural, likewise, Greek endings mark whether a noun is singular or plural (e.g. book, books).

Case:

In English we have three cases which are seen in how we use our pronouns.

1)
Subjective or Nominative Case: He=subject (e.g. He did it.)
2)
Objective or Accusative Case: Him = object (e.g. The car hit him.)
3)
Possessive or Genitive Case: His=possessive (e.g. It was his car.)

Greek adds two more:

4)
Dative: the case marking the indirect object (e.g. I told the story to the apostles.)
5)
Vocative: the case of direct address. (e.g. O Lord, save me.)

Endings will be added to the Greek nouns to indicate gender, number and case.

320.heading: Three Syllable Rules
320.text:
Three Syllable Rules
1)
There is one vowel or diphthong per syllable. A lone consonant often goes with the following vowel.
2)
Two consonants in a row are divided (except when the second consonant is ν or a consonant pair that is used to begin words).
3)
Two vowels (two diphthongs or a vowel and a diphthong) in a row are split unless the two vowels form a diphthong.

320.heading: 6 Accent Rules
320.text:
6 Accent Rules
1)
Nouns are retentive. They attempt to keep their accents on the same syllable.
2)
Verbs are recessive. Their accent recedes towards the first syllable as far as is possible.
3)
If the ultima is long, then the antepenult cannot be accented.
4)
If the ultima is long and the penult is accented, then the accent must be an acute.
5)
If the ultima is short and the penult is both long and accented, the accent must be a circumflex.
6)
If an acute is on the ultima, it becomes a grave when followed by another word.
(Machen, pp. 14f.; Mounce, p. 20)

Verbs are words of action or state of being.

topics.label: topic 2
topics.heading: Tense/Aspect
topics.text:
Tense/Aspect

Tense in English refers to the time of the action of the verb:

Present:  Annette swims.
Past:  Annette swam.
Future:  Annette will swim.

In Greek, tense is used to refer not only to time, (when the event happened), but also to aspect (the type of action).

topics.text:
Voice

English has two voices to which Greek adds a third:

Active voice: subject does the action of the verb.
Passive voice: subject receives the action of the verb.
Middle voice: where the subject acts on him/herself (reflexive) or members of a group interact among themselves (reciprocal). In Greek, self-interest may be reflected in the middle voice.

topics.label: topic 4
topics.heading: Mood
topics.text:
Mood

Mood refers to the kind of reality of the action, or how the action of the verb is regarded.

Indicative mood—simply states that something happened, e.g. Peter prays.
Imperative mood—gives a command or exhortation, e.g. Pray, Peter!
Subjunctive mood—expresses a wish, possibility or potentiality, e.g. Peter may pray.

topics.text:
Person

There are 3 persons in Greek.

First person is the person(s) speaking (I or we).
Second person is the person(s) spoken to (you [singular or plural]).
Third person is the person(s) or thing(s) spoken about (he, she, they, it).

topics.heading: Number and Agreement
topics.text:
Number and Agreement

Both English and Greek distinguish between singular (I, you, he, she, it) and the plural (we, you, they).

Verbs must agree with their subjects in both person and number.

He hits the ball.
They hit the ball.  (not "they hits the ball.")

Tense in English refers to the time of the action of the verb:

Present:  Annette swims.
Past:  Annette swam.
Future:  Annette will swim.

In Greek, tense is used to refer not only to time, (when the event happened), but also to aspect (the type of action).

Voice

English has two voices to which Greek adds a third:

Active voice: subject does the action of the verb.
Passive voice: subject receives the action of the verb.

Mood

Mood refers to the kind of reality of the action, or how the action of the verb is regarded.

Indicative mood—simply states that something happened, e.g. Peter prays.
Imperative mood—gives a command or exhortation, e.g. Pray, Peter!
Subjunctive mood—expresses a wish, possibility or potentiality, e.g. Peter may pray.

topics.text:
Movable Nu ( ν )

Sometimes a nu ( ν ) is added to the end of words ending in σι or ε, especially when it is followed by a word that begins with a vowel. In English we do something similar with "a book" and "an item." Thus sometimes the third plural form will be:

λύουσιν instead of λύουσι

topics.label: topic 5
topics.heading: Second Person Plural
topics.text:
Second Person Plural

In English we make no distinction between a "you" singular and a "you" which is plural ("you all"). Some grammars use "thou" for the singular and "ye" for the plural. Such usage is archaic and hence we will use "you" for both second person singular and plural. You should be aware that in Greek a sharp distinction is made.

(Machen, p. 22)

states.text:
Translation

The Present tense may denote either undefined (event simply happens) or continuous aspect (event was a process).

Thus it can be translated:

Undefined action: I loose, I run
Continuous action: I am loosing, I am running

The context will determine which should be used.

Historical Present

Greek will often use the present tense to reference an event that actually happened in the past. The historical present is used to add vividness to the narrative or, most often, it is an idiom. It often occurs in narrative in the third person. In these cases the present tense is simply translated by our past tense (e.g. "he says" becomes "he said").

(Mounce, p. 115; Machen, p. 20; Summers, pp. 12)

states.label: expander: Historical Present
states.heading: Translation
states.text:
Translation

The Present tense may denote either undefined (event simply happens) or continuous aspect (event was a process).

Thus it can be translated:

Undefined action: I loose, I run
Continuous action: I am loosing, I am running

The context will determine which should be used.

Historical Present

Greek will often use the present tense to reference an event that actually happened in the past. The historical present is used to add vividness to the narrative or, most often, it is an idiom. It often occurs in narrative in the third person. In these cases the present tense is simply translated by our past tense (e.g. "he says" becomes "he said").

(Mounce, p. 115; Machen, p. 20; Summers, pp. 12)

320.text:
Introduction

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We will learn the second declension first because it is more frequent. Second declension nouns are largely masculine which is indicated by placing a " ὁ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender. Second declension neuter nouns are marked by the definite article "τό ." The stem of second declension nouns end with an omicron.

topics.label: topic 2
topics.heading: Gender
topics.text:
Gender

Greek nouns are masculine, feminine, or neuter in gender. Often this gender is more a syntactic feature than a metaphysical statement as many inanimate objects are given grammatic gender. Thus "year" ( ἔτος ) is neuter while "day" ( ἡμέρα ) is feminine but "time" ( χρόνος ) is masculine. Gender is indicated by the definite article marker. It should be learned with the noun.

As in English, Greek has both singular and plural nouns. The verb must match the number of the subject noun the same way as in English:

The students love Greek.
The student loves Greek.

Inflectional Forms

There are 5 inflectional forms which mark the various cases or roles that nouns play in sentences.

Nominative form: marks the subject of the sentence.
Genitive form: expresses a possessive
Dative form: marks the indirect object
Accusative form: indicates the object of the sentence
Vocative form: is used for direct address

topics.label: topic 7
topics.heading: Word Order
topics.text:
Word Order

The order of words in a sentence in Greek is generally the same as in English (subject/verb/object). Greek puts inflectional endings on nouns in order to mark their case. This allows Greek to change the word order for various purposes. For example, the subject may be placed after the verb and the object placed before the verb for emphasis while retaining the original meaning of the sentence.

The stem of second declension nouns end with an omicron.

Declensions: First, Second, Third

A declension is a grouping of nouns that are inflected with a shared set of endings. The difference in endings does not affect the translation between first, second and third declensions. The second declension nouns are characterized by an "o" as the final letter of the stem. They are largely masculine or neuter. First declension nouns are characterized by an "η" or "α" and are mostly feminine. Third declension nouns have stems that end in a consonant.

First declension nouns are characterized by an "η" or "α" and are mostly feminine. Third declension nouns have stems that end in a consonant.

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We will learn the second declension first because it is more frequent. Second declension nouns are largely masculine which is indicated by placing a " ὁ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender. Second declension neuter nouns are marked by the definite article "τό ." The stem of second declension nouns end with an omicron.

Declensions: First, Second, Third
Definite Article

In contrast to English, which uses "a" as an indefinite article (e.g. "a book"), Greek has no indefinite article. Thus the Greek indefinite noun may be translated "book" or "a book." Greek nouns are assumed to be indefinite unless marked by the definite article ("the"). For now simply be aware of the nominative form of the definite article which will indicate the gender of the noun being learned:

= masculine ("the")
ἡ
= feminine ("the")
τό
= neuter ("the")

When you learn nouns you should remember which article goes with it as an indication of the noun's gender.

states.heading: Word Order
states.text:
Word Order

The order of words in a sentence in Greek is generally the same as in English (subject/verb/object). Greek puts inflectional endings on nouns in order to mark their case. This allows Greek to change the word order for various purposes. For example, the subject may be placed after the verb and the object placed before the verb for emphasis while retaining the original meaning of the sentence.

Thus "year" ( ἔτος ) is neuter while "day" ( ἡμέρα ) is feminine but "time" ( χρόνος ) is masculine. Gender is indicated by the definite article marker. It should be learned with the noun.

ὁ
= masculine (definite article = "the")
ἡ
= feminine
τό
= neuter

states.text:
Number and Agreement

As in English, Greek has both singular and plural nouns. The verb must match the number of the subject noun the same way as in English:

The students love Greek.
The student loves Greek.

Nominative form: marks the subject of the sentence.

Dative form: marks the indirect object

states.label: topic 7
states.heading: Word Order
states.text:
Word Order

The order of words in a sentence in Greek is generally the same as in English (subject/verb/object). Greek puts inflectional endings on nouns in order to mark their case. This allows Greek to change the word order for various purposes. For example, the subject may be placed after the verb and the object placed before the verb for emphasis while retaining the original meaning of the sentence.

topics.heading: Gender
topics.text:
Gender

Gender in English is determined by the sex of the referent: "king... he", female "queen... she". Objects which are neither male nor female are considered neuter: "boat...it". In Greek some inanimate objects are given male or female designations. Be careful not to confuse Greek grammatical gender with biological gender.

οἶκος
"house" is masculine
ἱερόν
"temple" is neuter
ἐκκλησία
"church" is feminine

topics.label: topic 5
topics.heading: Definite Article
topics.text:
Definite Article

In English we have both an indefinite article "a" (a book) and a definite article "the" (the book).

In Greek there is no indefinite article. Hence "book" and "a book" look exactly the same.

The definite article in Greek must match the noun it goes with in gender, number and case.

The definite article is to be learned with each noun as it will indicate the gender of the noun.

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We have learned the second declension with its masculine and neuter nouns. Now we will focus on the first declension which is largely feminine. First declension nouns are largely feminine which is indicated by placing a " ἡ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Declensions: First, Second, Third

A declension is a grouping of nouns that are inflected with a shared set of endings. The difference in endings does not effect the translation between first, second and third declensions. First declension nouns are characterized by an "η" or "α" and are mostly feminine. The second declension is characterized by an "o" as the final letter of the stem. They are largely masculine or neuter. Third declension nouns have stems that end in a consonant.

Definite Article

Greek has no indefinite article, whereas in English we would say "a book." Thus the Greek indefinite noun may be translated "book" or "a book." Greek nouns are assumed to be indefinite unless marked by the definite article ("the"). For now simply be aware of the nominative form of the definite article which will indicate the gender of the noun being learned:

= masculine ("the")
ἡ
= feminine ("the")
τό
= neuter ("the")

states.label: topic 1
states.heading: Introduction
states.text:
Introduction

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We have learned the second declension with its masculine and neuter nouns. Now we will focus on the first declension which is largely feminine. First declension nouns are largely feminine which is indicated by placing a " ἡ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender. The stem of first declension nouns end with an alpha or eta.

Declensions: First, Second, Third
Definite Article

states.label: expander: Declensions: First, Second, Third
states.heading: Introduction
states.text:
Introduction

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We have learned the second declension with its masculine and neuter nouns. Now we will focus on the first declension which is largely feminine. First declension nouns are largely feminine which is indicated by placing a " ἡ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender. The stem of first declension nouns end with an alpha or eta.

Declensions: First, Second, Third

A declension is a grouping of nouns that are inflected with a shared set of endings. The difference in endings does not effect the translation between first, second and third declensions. First declension nouns are characterized by an "η" or "α" and are mostly feminine. The second declension is characterized by an "o" as the final letter of the stem. They are largely masculine or neuter. Third declension nouns have stems that end in a consonant.

states.heading: Introduction
states.text:
Introduction

There are three noun declensions in Greek. We have learned the second declension with its masculine and neuter nouns. Now we will focus on the first declension which is largely feminine. First declension nouns are largely feminine which is indicated by placing a " ἡ " definite article ("the") in front of the root. Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender. The stem of first declension nouns end with an alpha or eta.

Declensions: First, Second, Third
Definite Article

Greek has no indefinite article, whereas in English we would say "a book." Thus the Greek indefinite noun may be translated "book" or "a book." Greek nouns are assumed to be indefinite unless marked by the definite article ("the"). For now simply be aware of the nominative form of the definite article which will indicate the gender of the noun being learned:

ὁ
= masculine ("the")
ἡ
= feminine ("the")
τό
= neuter ("the")

states.label: topic 2
states.heading: Gender
states.text:
Gender

Greek nouns are either masculine, feminine, or neuter in gender. Often this gender is more a syntactic feature than a metaphysical statement as many inanimate objects are given grammatic gender. Thus "year" ( ἔτος ) is neuter while "day" ( ἡμέρα ) is feminine but "time" ( χρόνος ) is masculine. Gender is indicated by the definite article marker which is to be learned with the noun.

ὁ
= masculine (definite article = "the")
ἡ
= feminine
τό
= neuter

states.label: topic 3
states.heading: Number and Agreement
states.text:
Number and Agreement

As in English, Greek has both singular and plural nouns. The verb must match the number of the subject noun the same way as in English:

The students love Greek.
The student loves Greek.

320.label: rail stop
320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

While Greek has no indefinite article like the English "a" (e.g. a book), the Greek definite article "the" occurs throughout the New Testament. The definite article will be inflected for gender, number and case. Indeed the definite article must match its noun in gender, number and case. The definite article will mark the gender of a noun no matter if it is a first, second or third declension noun.

320.text:
Definition

Prepositions are usually small words that link or relate two words together. Often they tell position in space or time.

Put the book on the table.
Tells of the spatial relationship of the book to the table.
He went after the game.
Connects the person's going to the time of the game.

320.label: rail stop
320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

Greek prepositions are connecting or linking words like English prepositions. Each preposition will take a noun in a certain case (genitive, dative, or accusative). This case must be learned along with the preposition's main meaning(s). The most common meanings are listed with each preposition but it is important to observe the context as many other meanings are possible.

Note that the genitive often has the idea of separation, the dative the idea of location, and the accusative motion toward.

topics.label: topic 7
topics.heading: Proclitics
topics.text:
Proclitics

A proclitic is a word that has no accent because it is joined so closely with the accented word that follows it. ἐν, εἰς and ἐκ are proclitics.

They come before (pro) the word with the accent.

Enclitics are accentless words that follow the word with the accent. Personal pronouns are often enclitics.

Compounds

Prepositions are often found compounded with a verb in Greek. Sometimes the meaning of the compound may be determined by combining the meaning of the preposition with the meaning of the verb. Other times, however, the preposition affects the meaning of the verb in other ways, such as intensifying it.

topics.label: topic 7
topics.heading: Proclitics
topics.text:
Proclitics

A proclitic is a word that has no accent because it is joined so closely with the accented word that follows it. ἐν, εἰς and ἐκ are proclitics.

They come before (pro) the word with the accent.

Enclitics are accentless words that follow the word with the accent. Personal pronouns are often enclitics.

320.text:
Definition

An adjective is a word used to modify a noun or pronoun. The adjective often specifies more clearly what the noun or pronoun actually means. It often answers the question "What kind of ______ is it?"

The soft snow hit the windshield.
    Answers:  what kind of snow?  soft
The snow was soft.

topics.heading: 3 Uses of Adjectives
topics.text:
3 Uses of Adjectives

Adjectives are used in 3 ways:

Attributive: the adjective attributes a characteristic to the noun it modifies.
The good book
Predicate: the adjective assigns a characteristic to the subject of the sentence.
The book is good.
Substantive: the adjective acts independently as a noun itself.
The good die young.

320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. They will match the nouns they modify in number, gender and case.

Adjectives frequently use a 2-1-2 paradigm:

masculine = 2nd declension forms,
feminine = 1st declension forms, and
neuter = 2nd declension forms.

When an adjective's root ends in an epsilon, iota, or rho, the "a" 1st declension form will be used.

topics.heading: Substantive Use
topics.text:
Substantive Use

The substantive use of the adjective is when the adjective is used as a noun. The substantive use often has the article.

οἱ δὲ δίκαιοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον
and the righteous unto eternal life
Mat 25:46
Ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται
and the righteous will live by faith
Rom 1:17

Sometimes neither the adjective nor the noun has the article in which case context must determine whether to translate it attributively or predicatively.

Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns. They will match the nouns they modify in number, gender and case.

320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

εἰμί is a stative verb (it indicates a state of being) and so has no voice (active, middle, passive).

In English "is" takes a predicate nominative rather than the normal accusative. It is correct to say "This is he" and incorrect to say "This is him." Similarly in Greek a noun or pronoun in the nominative follows the verb εἰμί.

topics.heading: οὐ, οὐκ and οὐχ
topics.text:
οὐ, οὐκ and οὐχ

οὐ is placed before the word it negates which is usually the verb. There are three forms of this word depending on the initial letter of the word that follows it:

1)
οὐ before a consonant;
2)
οὐκ before a vowel with a smooth breathing mark; and
3)
οὐχ before a vowel with a rough breathing mark.

Definition

A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun usually for brevity or to avoid repetition. The person or object to which the pronoun refers is called its "antecedent."

Zach threw the ball to Elliott.
It (the ball) hit him (Elliott) in the head.

topics.heading: Types of Pronouns
topics.text:
Types of Pronouns

There are various types of Pronouns:

Personal pronouns: stand in for a person—"Bill did it. He was there."
Demonstrative pronouns: point to a person or object which is near (this/these) or far (that/those).
Relative pronouns: relate a subordinate clause to a noun—"It is a great person who attempts to master Greek."
Reciprocal pronouns: state an interchange between two things/persons—They loved one another.
Reflexive pronouns: direct the action of the verb back to the subject—"She hid herself behind the door."
Interrogative pronouns: ask a question—Who broke the chair?

In English, pronouns have three cases:

Subjective—which are used when a pronoun is the subject of a sentence (He turned left).
Possessive—which are used to indicate ownership (He gave his best).
Objective—which are used when a pronoun is the object of a sentence (He left him).

320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

Personal pronouns in Greek will match their antecedent in person, gender, and number. The case will be determined by the role the pronoun plays in the sentence.

Personal pronouns will be either first person (I, we), second person (you), or third person (he/she/it/they).

Greek will use the genitive where we would normally use a possessive pronoun (e.g. his, her).

Since the nominative is indicated in the personal ending of the verb (e.g. λέγω = I say) when the personal pronoun is used it is for emphasis (e.g. ἐγὼ λέγω = I say).

In the first and second person there are emphatic forms. These are usually the forms used in prepositional phrases.

topics.label: topic 5
topics.heading: Enclitics
topics.text:
Enclitics

An enclitic is a word that is phonetically attached so closely with the word that precedes it that it has no accent of its own. Many personal pronouns are enclitics (e.g. μου, μοι, με, σου, σοι, σε).

Enclitics are sometimes accented:

for emphasis
when the first word in a sentence.

If the preceding word has an acute on the antepenult or a circumflex on the penult, a second accent will be added on the ultima. This results in the word preceding the enclitic being double accented.

ἄνθρωπός μου
my man
δῶρόν σου
your gift

Finally, an acute on the ultima is not changed to a grave before an enclitic.

The third person pronoun αὐτός differs from the first and second person pronouns in that it is marked for gender. With first and second person pronouns, there is no need to specify gender because it is understood as the one speaking or one being spoken to.

αὐτός also has some other special features which we will examine here.

As a pronoun—matching its antecedent in number and gender and translated as "he," "she," "it," or "they."
Reflexive Intensifier—when it is used as an adjective in the predicate position (usually in the nominative case) it is translated reflexively (e.g. he himself will get the car).
Adjective meaning "same"—when it is used as an adjective in the attributive position, it is translated as "same."

320.heading: Definitions
320.text:
Definitions

There are two voices in English. The active voice is where the subject of the sentence does the action. "Zach hits the ball."

The passive voice is where the subject is acted on by the verb. "Zach was hit by the ball."

Greek adds a third voice, the middle voice, which we will look at shortly.

topics.label: topic 2
topics.heading: Identifying Traits
topics.text:
Identifying Traits

A passive verb often can be identified by placing a "by what" after the verb.

"Zach is hit by the ball."

"Zach is hit by what?" — the ball.

Zach is the subject being acted on. The ball is the agent doing the action.

topics.label: topic 3
topics.heading: Translation
topics.text:
Translation

The present tense may describe punctiliar action (single point in time: He hit the ball) or continuous action (He is hitting the ball). When the passive is used a helping verb carries the tense of the verb.

He is hit by the ball. — present punctiliar
He is being hit by the ball — present cont.
He was hit by the ball. — past
He will be hit by the ball. — future

Introduction

The present middle and passive have exactly the same form. The context must be examined to determine which is being used. There are approximately three times as many passive as middle verbs in the New Testament. A helping verb is used when translating passives. The helping verb indicates whether the verb is being taken in a punctiliar or continuous manner.

The middle has several functions:

deponent: where the middle is translated as active. Most middles (75%) are deponent and should be translated as an active. "Tanya splashed Rebekah."
the subject does an action on the object but it in turn impacts the subject. (Mounce, pp. 149, 224)
self-interest "Tanya splashed herself."

topics.label: topic 4
topics.heading: Deponent Verbs
topics.text:
Deponent Verbs

Deponent verbs are verbs that are middle in form but translated as actives. They have no active form and are easy to tell in vocabulary lists because they have the middle ending -ομαι.

Mounce notes that in the New Testament about 75% of the middle forms are deponent (p. 149).

Because of the deponent phenomena, middle forms may frequently be translated as actives (3 to 1). Many frequent verbs are deponent.

When parsing a deponent verb, rather than listing the voice as active/middle/ passive, the verb is said to be deponent (e.g. present deponent indicative 1 sg).

topics.label: topic 5
topics.heading: Accompanying Cases
topics.text:
Accompanying Cases

Often with passives there is a need to express the agent, instrument, or means by which the subject is acted on.

This is accomplished by:

using ὑπό or διά with the genitive to expresses agency (e.g. Elliott was hit by Zach.) or
using the dative case to indicate means or instrument. The translation will use "with" or "by" (e.g. Elliott was hit by the ball.).

topics.text:
Compound Verbs

As with other verbs, prepositions are often prefixed to deponent verbs to form a compound.

ἔρχομαι
I go in, enter
εἰσέρχομαι
I go in, enter (εἰς)
ἐξέρχομαι
I go out, leave (ἐκ)
διέρχομαι
I go through (διά)

In the past we say,
     "We went to college."

In the future we say,
     "We will go to college."

320.heading: Introduction
320.text:
Introduction

In the present tense in Greek we have seen that aspect, rather than time, is the focus. The future tense in Greek specifies that the action of the verb takes place in the future. This is similar to the future tense in English. Summers notes three functions of the future tense in Greek (p. 67):

predictive (e.g. "We will go.")
imperative (e.g. "You shall go.") or
deliberative with rhetorical questions (e.g. "to whom shall we go?").

The future tense is easy to remember as the endings are the same as the present. The difference is a sigma which is usually added between the stem and the ending.

Stem + Sigma + Ending
λύ + σ + ω
(λύσω — I will loose)

The future passive will be learned later as it is built off a different stem.

topics.heading: 5 Stem Variations
topics.text:
5 Stem Variations

The adding of the sigma may change the final consonant of the verb stem in the following three ways:

if after a palatal ( κ, γ, χ )
σ + [ κ, γ, χ] ==> ξ
if after a labial ( π, β, φ )
σ + [ π, β, φ] ==> ψ
if after a dental ( τ, δ, θ )
σ + [ τ, δ, θ ] ==> σ
if after a liquid ( λ, μ, ν, ρ ) the sigma is dropped and the ω is accented with a circumflex. When a stem ends in a double liquid consonant, one of them is sometimes dropped.
if after a sibilant ( σ, ζ ) the sibilant is dropped and the sigma is kept.

768.label: rail stop
768.heading: Introduction
768.text:
Introduction

In the present tense in Greek we have seen that aspect, rather than time, is the focus. The future tense in Greek specifies that the action of the verb takes place in the future. This is similar to the future tense in English. Summers notes three functions of the future tense in Greek (p. 67):

predictive (e.g. "We will go.")
imperative (e.g. "You shall go.") or
deliberative with rhetorical questions (e.g. "to whom shall we go?").

The future tense is easy to remember as the endings are the same as the present. The difference is a sigma which is usually added between the stem and the ending.

Stem + Sigma + Ending
λύ + σ + ω
(λύσω — I will loose)

The future passive will be learned later as it is built off a different stem.

Next Topic

deliberative with rhetorical questions (e.g. "to whom shall we go?").
